record.original_question: Is there a positive integer k such that the system (S) is equivalent to one of its subsystems induced by q equations?

evidence.quote: Is there a positive integer k such that the system (S) is equivalent to one of its subsystems induced by q equations?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet and let $\Sigma^*$ denote the free monoid generated by $\Sigma$. For a finite set of unknowns $X = \{x_1, \dots, x_n\}$, a word equation is a pair $(u, v) \in (X \cup \Sigma)^* \times (X \cup \Sigma)^*$, usually written $u = v$. A morphism $h : (X \cup \Sigma)^* \to \Sigma^*$ that fixes every letter of $\Sigma$ is called a solution of the equation $u = v$ if $h(u) = h(v)$. A (possibly infinite) system $S$ of word equations on the unknowns $X$ is the conjunction of all its equations, and a solution of $S$ is a morphism that solves every equation in $S$. Two systems are said to be equivalent if they have exactly the same set of solutions. A subsystem of $S$ is any subset $S' \subseteq S$.

By the compactness theorem for free monoids (Ehrenfeucht's conjecture), every system $S$ of word equations on finitely many unknowns over $\Sigma^*$ is equivalent to some finite subsystem of itself. The question is whether this finite bound can be made uniform: 

Does there exist a positive integer $k$, depending only on the number $n$ of unknowns (and possibly on $|\Sigma|$), such that every system $S$ of word equations on $n$ unknowns over $\Sigma^*$ is equivalent to one of its subsystems consisting of at most $k$ equations?
artifact.status_search_result: Ehrenfeucht's compactness property (proved by Albert–Lawrence and Guba) guarantees that every infinite system of word equations on finitely many unknowns is equivalent to a finite subsystem, but no uniform bound on the size of such a subsystem in terms of the number of unknowns is known. For three unknowns the best known upper bound is 18 (Saarela, 2018), with the conjectured value being 3, and for $n \geq 4$ unknowns there exist independent systems of size $\Theta(n^4)$ but no finite upper bound is known. The general question therefore remains open.

status_evidence.title: Independent Systems of Word Equations: From Ehrenfeucht to Eighteen
status_evidence.snippet: For three-variable equations the maximal size of an independent system is at most 18; this is the first such finite upper bound.
status_evidence.claim: For three unknowns a finite upper bound is now known, but the general uniform-bound question remains open.

status_evidence.title: Ehrenfeucht conjecture - Encyclopedia of Mathematics
status_evidence.snippet: Every system of equations on finitely many unknowns over a free monoid is equivalent to a finite subsystem.
status_evidence.claim: Ehrenfeucht's conjecture (compactness) is proved, but no uniform size bound is asserted.

status_evidence.title: On Maximal Chains of Systems of Word Equations
status_evidence.snippet: The question of the maximal size of an independent system of word equations on n unknowns is open for n>=3.
status_evidence.claim: The uniform-bound problem is explicitly stated as open.
